conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Sarah, a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you adjust to life with your new baby.

Over the next few minutes we’ll use a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s a 10-item screening that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. Many new parents find it helpful to pause, reflect, and put words to the ups and downs of new motherhood.

Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers. If at any point you need a break or want to talk further, just let me know. We’ll go through the questions one at a time, and I’ll ask them conversationally—no need to remember any numbers or categories.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first question:

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[Lets out a small sigh, eyes downcast]

Mostly it’s felt… difficult. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday—normally I’d have cracked up—but I just stared at it and handed the phone back to my husband. I did manage a tiny laugh when the baby made a goofy milk-bubble face, but even that felt kind of muted, like I’m watching happiness through frosted glass.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[Shakes head slowly, voice soft]

No… not really. I mean, I can force a little chuckle when my husband tries to joke, but it doesn’t feel real. It’s like the laughter gets stuck somewhere in my chest before it ever reaches me.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[Wrapping the receiving blanket tighter around her fingers]

Not much… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now I mostly think “what’s the point?” I still go through the motions, hoping the enjoyment will click back in, but it feels flat, like I’m watching myself from outside.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Voice drops, eyes fixed on the baby’s empty bottle]

Yeah… I do that a lot. If he spits up more than usual, my brain jumps straight to “I must’ve eaten something wrong.” When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept thinking, “A good mom would know the trick—why can’t I figure it out?” I know, rationally, babies just cry, but the guilt still lands on me every single time.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[Presses fingertips to temples]

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly picture him choking—even though he’s latched fine—and my heart starts racing. Or I’ll lie awake convinced the ceiling fan is going to fall on the crib. I know it’s unlikely, but the worry just barges in and circles like a moth I can’t swat away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes... like yesterday, I was just rocking him in the glider and out of nowhere my chest got tight, heart pounding, couldn't catch my breath. Nothing had happened—he was asleep on my shoulder—but for a minute I felt like the room was closing in. It passed after a bit, but it left me shaky the rest of the afternoon.
Things have been getting on top of me

[Nods slowly, voice shaky]

Yes... most days it feels like I'm drowning in small tasks. The laundry pile looks like a mountain, and when he starts to fuss I think, "I can't do this again." I still get up and manage, but it's like walking through waist-deep water—every step takes so much effort.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[Exhales, rubbing her eyes]

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed myself, and then my brain starts replaying every little thing I might’ve done wrong—did I burp him long enough, why did he cry longer today, am I already failing him? The thoughts just loop until I’m wide awake, and even when I do drift off I jerk awake at the slightest sound, heart racing.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Shoulders sag, eyes glassy]

Yeah… a lot of the time. It’s like a gray fog parked over everything. I’ll be holding him and still feel this heaviness in my chest. Some mornings I wake up already feeling like I’m on the verge of tears, and I don’t even know why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Presses lips together, voice cracks]

Twice this week. Yesterday I set the bottle down a little too hard and the milk sloshed out—such a dumb thing—but I just burst into tears at the counter. And the night before, he wouldn’t settle for almost an hour; when he finally fell asleep I sat on the floor outside his room and cried quietly so my husband wouldn’t hear.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[Swallows hard, looking down at her hands]

It... flickered through my head a couple of times. Nothing planned—just this quick picture of "what if I weren't here." I shove it away right away because I don't ever want to leave him, but the thought still popped up, especially on the nights when I'm exhausted and feel like I'm failing him.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant 3–4 wks old (per clinical context)  
Date: [today]

1. Endorsed symptoms (EPDS-anchored paraphrase)  
- Anhedonia, low mood, crying spells nearly daily  
- Marked loss of enjoyment (“flat,” “watching myself from outside”)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care  
- Intruding, irrational worries; nocturnal rumination  
- Discrete panic-like episode (tight chest, breathlessness)  
- Feeling overwhelmed; “drowning in small tasks”  
- Initial insomnia and restless, hyper-vigilant sleep  
- Passive self-harm cognition (“what if I weren’t here” – no plan/intent)

2. Observed signs  
Slowed speech, tearfulness, avoids eye contact, persistent fatigue

3. Pattern  
Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, for ≥2 wks; interfere with functioning and attachment

4. Risk flags  
– Passive suicidal ideation (low frequency, no intent)  
– Moderate-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms  
– Impaired sleep and coping

5. Screening conclusion  
High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; safety plan and immediate follow-up assessment warranted.
